papers.title: Lambda-Hold Control: Human-Like Movement Emerges from a Minimal Task Reward in Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulation
papers.code_status: Not released. Project page shows 'Code (TBA)' (site last commit 2026-08-21); no Lambda-Hold repo under the first or second author's GitHub; checked 2026-09-23.
papers.api_title: Lambda-Hold Control: Human-Like Movement Emerges from a Minimal Task Reward in Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulation
papers.core_idea: The policy outputs a stretch-reflex threshold lambda per muscle (0.6-1.2 optimal fibre lengths). A fixed law, e = clip01(50(l-lambda) + 0.1*max(v,0)), produces excitations. Lambda is held between GRF events (0.05-0.15 s holds). SAC+gSDE on H2190 reaches about 4.7 m/s.
papers.what_to_take: Take the exact recruitment law, gains, lambda bounds, GRF trigger and sub-point, 432-D sensory observation, and reward exp(vx)*exp(-(vz/0.1)^2) with its terminations. Also the four baselines and the RSI archive against sprint forgetting.
papers.left_untested: Tested only on H2190 in SCONE/Hyfydy at 0.01 s, two seeds per curve. No reflex delays, arms or fatigue, and no MuJoCo/MyoLeg port. The 6.5 m/s run doubled shortening velocity and is diagnostic only.
papers.feasibility_notes: About 4.0 m/s after ~1 h on an RTX 5070 with Hyfydy. The MuJoCo plant differs, so re-derive lambda bounds and gains. Code unreleased.

papers.title: Learning Realistic Athletic Sprinting Without Demonstrations
papers.authors_short: Wang, Bianco, Tevet et al. (Hicks, Liu, Delp, Fatahalian)
papers.code_status: Released: Bolt simulator (github.com/willwng/bolt, pushed 2026-08-26) plus RL envs with FastTD3/QFlex/SAC/PPO configs (github.com/willwng/msk_envs). GitHub reports no licence file; checked 2026-09-23.
papers.api_title: Learning Realistic Athletic Sprinting Without Demonstrations
papers.core_idea: Bolt, a Warp GPU simulator, reproduces OpenSim muscle-tendon dynamics at about 1000x real time. FastTD3 drives 136 muscle excitations directly at 30 Hz, rewarded only for speed, joint-limit pain and staying alive. The model runs a full 100 m, peaking at 12.5 m/s.
papers.what_to_take: A direct-excitation baseline recipe. Off-policy TD3/SAC beat PPO. Default noise sufficed; gSDE and DEP gave no gain. Five seeds reached 98-101 m in 10 s. Swapping force-based contacts/limits for MuJoCo's solver prevented realistic sprinting.
papers.left_untested: Lower-body maximum isometric forces were doubled, so 12.5 m/s breaks your strength rule. The paper models no fatigue and runs no reward-matched comparison with Lambda-Hold. It tests neither MyoLeg nor a device.
papers.feasibility_notes: Runs on one GPU; model parsing needs OpenSim from conda. Whether H2190 (an OpenSim conversion exists) loads in Bolt is untested.

papers.title: Natural and Robust Walking using Reinforcement Learning without Demonstrations in High-Dimensional Musculoskeletal Models (published as: Emergence of natural and robust bipedal walking by learning from biologically plausible objectives)
papers.venue: iScience 28(4):112203 (2025), journal title 'Emergence of natural and robust bipedal walking by learning from biologically plausible objectives'; arXiv 2023
papers.code_status: Released (MIT). Includes Hyfydy/sconegym configs and pretrained baselines, plus the MyoLeg DEP-RL baseline via MyoSuite. The MyoLeg natural-walking cost-term tutorial is still 'promised'.
papers.api_title: Natural and Robust Walking using Reinforcement Learning without Demonstrations in High-Dimensional Musculoskeletal Models
papers.core_idea: DEP-RL with an adaptive effort-cost reward learns natural, robust walking without demonstrations. Models: H0918, H1622 and H2190 in Hyfydy, plus the 80-muscle MyoLeg in MuJoCo. An arXiv appendix adds maximum-speed running on every model, rewarded by centre-of-mass velocity.
papers.what_to_take: The only MyoLeg maximum-speed RL result found: 5.44 m/s, against 6.49 m/s for H2190. MyoLeg runs with strong lateral torso oscillation. Reuse their reward terms, self-collision penalty and configs.
papers.left_untested: Speeds are the best of 20 rollouts, not seed medians. Hyfydy models were strengthened to MyoLeg force levels for running. Running kinematics depart from human data. No sprint start, fatigue or held actions.
papers.feasibility_notes: pip install deprl. The MyoLeg path needs no Hyfydy licence; the H-model configs do (the trial licence ends 2026-09-25).

papers.title: DEP-RL: Embodied Exploration for Reinforcement Learning in Overactuated and Musculoskeletal Systems
papers.code_status: Released (MIT); pip package deprl; MPO-based; MyoSuite ships a DEP-RL MyoLeg baseline.
papers.api_title: DEP-RL: Embodied Exploration for Reinforcement Learning in Overactuated and Musculoskeletal Systems
papers.core_idea: DEP (differential extrinsic plasticity) is a self-organising sensorimotor rule. During data collection it periodically takes over action selection, so exploration covers the state space within seconds on overactuated muscle systems. Paired with MPO, it learns reaching and locomotion, including running with a 120-muscle ostrich.
papers.what_to_take: The MyoLeg-proven exploration baseline for a direct-excitation human. Lambda-Hold rescaled DEP time windows by 2.5 for a 0.01 s step and reached only about 2.6 m/s, with a gait that did not look human-like.
papers.left_untested: Sprint quality. Lambda-Hold saw trunk lean and asymmetry; Bolt saw shorter episodes and no gain. DEP combined with lambda-space or held actions is untested.
papers.feasibility_notes: CPU-parallel MPO; the hyperparameters depend on the simulation step. Start from MyoSuite's pretrained MyoLeg DEP-RL baseline.

papers.title: Smooth Exploration for Robotic Reinforcement Learning
papers.code_status: Released (MIT) in Stable-Baselines3 via the use_sde and sde_sample_freq options.
papers.api_title: Smooth Exploration for Robotic Reinforcement Learning
papers.core_idea: Generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE) makes action noise a function of policy features, with the noise matrix resampled every n steps. Exploration becomes smooth and temporally consistent, trading performance for smoothness. Tested on PyBullet tasks and three real robots.
papers.what_to_take: This is Lambda-Hold's exploration setting: SAC+gSDE in SB3, resampled every 4 decision steps. Keep it identical for the replication gate and treat sample frequency as a sensitivity parameter.
papers.left_untested: No musculoskeletal system was tested. Bolt reports no sprint gain from gSDE. With event-length holds, noise changes per decision rather than per unit time, and that effect is unstudied.
papers.feasibility_notes: Zero cost: one SB3 flag for SAC or PPO.

papers.title: Muscle Synergy Priors Enhance Biomechanical Fidelity in Predictive Musculoskeletal Locomotion Simulation
papers.code_status: No code found. The project page has videos only (ces40320.github.io/WebHomepage__Walk-RL); checked 2026-09-23.
papers.api_title: Muscle Synergy Priors Enhance Biomechanical Fidelity in Predictive Musculoskeletal Locomotion Simulation
papers.core_idea: NMF synergies come from inverse analysis of a few walking trials, using H2190 converted to OpenSim. They form the SAC action space in Hyfydy, with phase-based mirroring. Gait is stable at 0.7-1.8 m/s and on ±6° slopes, with fewer non-physiological knee patterns than unconstrained control.
papers.what_to_take: Same lab as Lambda-Hold (H2190, SB3 SAC, 75M steps on an RTX 4090, five seeds) and the source of its synergy baseline. A template for a low-dimensional human action space and for reporting five seeds.
papers.left_untested: The authors did not test running or sprinting. The basis comes from walking inverse dynamics, not EMG, and is fixed. MuJoCo/MyoLeg transfer is untested.
papers.feasibility_notes: Needs inverse-analysis data and Hyfydy. Alternatively distil a basis from your own sprint rollouts, as Lambda-Hold did.

papers.title: Reflex-Informed Neuromuscular Reinforcement Learning for Muscle-Driven Locomotion
papers.code_status: No code link in the paper or on GitHub search; checked 2026-09-23.
papers.api_title: Reflex-Informed Neuromuscular Reinforcement Learning for Muscle-Driven Locomotion
papers.core_idea: A fixed, phase-dependent reflex controller stimulates the muscles. An RL policy outputs four residual parameters that modulate hip-swing, knee-support and ankle-propulsion reflex gains and thresholds from the current state. Setup: Hyfydy via SCONE Gym, sagittal H0918v2j model, walking at 0.8-1.2 m/s.
papers.what_to_take: A low-dimensional, interpretable residual-on-reflex interface, tested head to head against end-to-end RL and DEP-RL. It stays robust to muscle weakness and pushes without retraining. A possible third human arm beside excitation and lambda control.
papers.left_untested: Only planar walking up to 1.2 m/s. No running, 3D model, MuJoCo port or Lambda-Hold comparison. The reflex phases are hand-designed for walking and lack a flight phase.
papers.feasibility_notes: The four-dimensional action is cheap to learn. Adding sprint phases, including flight, to the reflex state machine is the real work.

papers.title: MuscleVAE: Model-Based Controllers of Muscle-Actuated Characters
papers.code_status: Released (linked from the project page); GitHub reports no licence; last push 2024-03.
papers.api_title: MuscleVAE: Model-Based Controllers of Muscle-Actuated Characters
papers.core_idea: A full-body Hill-type character carries 3CC-r fatigue in every muscle. The policy sets per-muscle target lengths that PD servos track. A VAE skill latent is trained model-based on about 25 min of motion capture, including running, and motion style shifts as fatigue builds and recovers.
papers.what_to_take: Two precedents. First, a learned length-referent action space (lambda-like; not cited by Lambda-Hold). Second, full-body 3CC-r fatigue in which running weakens, then recovers during walking or standing.
papers.left_untested: It imitates motion capture rather than predicting from a minimal reward. Targets are re-set every step with no holds. Fatigue parameters are not calibrated for sprinting, and sprint speed and EMG are not validated.
papers.feasibility_notes: Unoptimised training took about a week on CPU plus an RTX 3090. Borrow the fatigue integration, not the pipeline.

papers.title: Modification of a three-compartment muscle fatigue model to predict peak torque decline during intermittent tasks
papers.code_status: Implemented in MyoSuite as CumulativeFatigue (myosuite/envs/myo/fatigue.py; added in v2.4.0, 2024-05-13; MJX variant exists). KINESIS reuses it.
papers.api_title: Modification of a three-compartment muscle fatigue model to predict peak torque decline during intermittent tasks
papers.core_idea: Adds a rest-recovery multiplier r to the three-compartment (resting, active, fatigued) fatigue model, so recovery speeds up during rest intervals. Against intermittent-task data from 63 publications, prediction error in torque decline fell from 19-29% to 6-10%.
papers.what_to_take: The fatigue model MyoSuite already applies to MyoLeg muscles. You need it to test assistance over the second 100 m, where the human exosuit study found no significant gain.
papers.left_untested: Fitted to isometric and intermittent joint-torque tasks; MyoSuite's default F, R and r come from elbow data. Maximal sprint fatigue over about 25 s is uncalibrated, and the model has no locomotion validation.
papers.feasibility_notes: Negligible compute. Per-muscle F, R and r must be set or fitted to sprint power-decline data.

papers.title: Running Speed is Maximized by Strengthening the Hip Flexors and Hip Adductors
papers.api_title: Running Speed is Maximized by Strengthening the Hip Flexors and Hip Adductors
papers.core_idea: Full-body musculoskeletal dynamic optimisation ranks how much each leg muscle's strength drives maximum sprint speed. A 10% hip-strength gain adds 2.59% speed, mainly through step frequency, against 1.02% for the ankle and 0.33% for the knee. Hip flexors are the most sensitive group.
papers.what_to_take: Shows why the no-strength-increase rule matters and where assistance has the most leverage: hip flexion. This agrees with Lambda-Hold's finding that hip-flexor force-velocity limits its top speed.
papers.left_untested: Uses optimal control, not a learned controller, and varies strength rather than adding external hip torque. Covers top speed only, not a 200 m race with acceleration and fatigue.
papers.feasibility_notes: No compute. Use as a prior on exosuit torque direction and to sanity-check simulated sensitivities.

papers.title: Where Entropy Is Measured Matters: Policy Geometry in Bounded Continuous-Control PPO
papers.code_status: The paper describes an archival code package and promises a public repository; no URL found; checked 2026-09-23.
papers.api_title: Where Entropy Is Measured Matters: Policy Geometry in Bounded Continuous-Control PPO
papers.core_idea: In PPO on 80-muscle MyoLeg walking, a clipped Gaussian sends 89% of actions within 5% of a bound; most policy means sit outside the executable range. Measuring entropy on executed actions pulls means inward: near-bound occupancy falls from 71% to 19% (three seeds).
papers.what_to_take: A diagnostic for a direct-excitation MyoLeg human: log the fraction of near-bound excitations and the mean geometry. SAC already measures entropy on executed actions; SMAT's PPO stages do not.
papers.left_untested: Three MyoLeg seeds, walking only. Matched geometry can still differ in return. No sprinting, SAC/TD3 comparison or lambda-space actions, and no assessment of whether bang-bang excitations are plausible.
papers.feasibility_notes: A cheap logging diagnostic; applies directly to the PPO actors in SMAT-style co-adaptation.

papers.title: TempoRL: Learning When to Act
papers.core_idea: The agent picks an action and also how long to commit to it. A skip-policy learned over skip connections between states repeats the action, which learns up to ten times faster than vanilla Q-learning.
papers.what_to_take: A learned alternative to Lambda-Hold's hand-set GRF trigger: let the policy choose hold length within 0.05-0.15 s. Compare against event-triggered holds on the same step budget.
papers.left_untested: Tested on tabular and deep RL benchmarks, not musculoskeletal or contact-rich locomotion. It repeats a frozen action, whereas lambda-holds keep reflexes running. Interaction with SAC entropy tuning is unknown.
papers.feasibility_notes: Adds a small skip-policy head; negligible compute.

papers.title: SAR: Generalization of Physiological Agility and Dexterity via Synergistic Action Representation
papers.code_status: MyoSuite ships a pretrained MyoLeg locomotion SAR (PCA/ICA/normaliser in myosuite/agents/SAR_pretrained) with a tutorial notebook.
papers.api_title: SAR: Generalization of Physiological Agility and Dexterity via Synergistic Action Representation
papers.core_idea: Synergies are extracted (PCA, then ICA) from policies trained on simpler tasks and reused as a low-dimensional action representation for harder ones. MyoLeg learns robust locomotion over stairs and hills in 4M steps, where end-to-end RL failed, and generalises zero-shot.
papers.what_to_take: A ready-made MyoLeg synergy action space, and a pipeline for distilling synergies from your own trained runner. It is the MuJoCo counterpart to Park's Hyfydy synergy baseline.
papers.left_untested: Terrain locomotion only; no running or sprinting reported. The fixed synergy basis cannot adapt online, and there is no reflex or hold interface. Synergies from slow gaits may miss sprint coordination.
papers.feasibility_notes: Runs in MyoSuite's CPU simulation; SAR adds only a linear map.

papers.title: A neural circuitry that emphasizes spinal feedback generates diverse behaviours of human locomotion
papers.api_title: A neural circuitry that emphasizes spinal feedback generates diverse behaviours of human locomotion
papers.core_idea: Ten spinal muscle-reflex modules and a supraspinal layer that sets foot placement and chooses the swing leg. With neural delays and musculotendon dynamics but no central pattern generator, the model produces 3D walking, running, speed changes, slopes, stairs, turning and obstacle avoidance.
papers.what_to_take: Evidence that reflex feedback alone can generate 3D running. Also a checklist of reflex ingredients Lambda-Hold omits: transmission delays, force feedback and phase-specific modules.
papers.left_untested: Gains are hand-structured and optimised per behaviour. Sprint speeds, learned high-level control and interaction with external devices are not addressed.
papers.feasibility_notes: Porting to MuJoCo is moderate work; learned residual modulation, as in arXiv 2609.11733, avoids hand-tuning per behaviour.

papers.title: Once More on the Equilibrium-Point Hypothesis (λ Model) for Motor Control
papers.api_title: Once More on the Equilibrium-Point Hypothesis (λ Model) for Motor Control
papers.core_idea: The tonic stretch-reflex threshold lambda is the central command. Lambda, the muscle's invariant characteristic and the load together fix an equilibrium point, so one mechanism governs posture and movement. The reflex drives the limb to a load-dependent equilibrium; it does not track a prescribed length.
papers.what_to_take: The theory behind Lambda-Hold's control variable: lambda sets where a muscle starts resisting stretch, not a length target. This matters when interpreting learned lambda sequences or porting them across models.
papers.left_untested: Built for single joints and posture, not learning, locomotion or high-speed dynamics. Where lambda commands come from is left open, the 'homunculus' objection raised again in 2026.
papers.feasibility_notes: Theory only. Read the sections on the invariant characteristic and recruitment before fixing lambda bounds.

papers.title: Limitations to maximum sprinting speed imposed by muscle mechanical properties
papers.api_title: Limitations to maximum sprinting speed imposed by muscle mechanical properties
papers.core_idea: 2D Hill-muscle forward-dynamics sprint simulations remove one muscle property at a time. Without force-velocity, top speed rises 15%; without activation dynamics, 8%; without force-length, 4%. Removing tendon elasticity lowers it 26%.
papers.what_to_take: Explains Lambda-Hold's hip-flexor ceiling and why its 6.5 m/s run, with doubled shortening velocity, falls outside your gate. Activation dynamics also cap speed, so keep MyoLeg time constants at their defaults.
papers.left_untested: A 2D, optimisation-based simulation, not learned feedback control. No 3D balance, arms, learned policies or assistive devices.
papers.feasibility_notes: No compute. Use it to fix which MyoLeg muscle parameters must stay frozen.

cluster_lessons: Three demonstration-free RL results give muscle-driven top speeds. Lambda-Hold reached about 4.7 m/s on H2190 at default strength (two seeds). Bolt reached 12.5 m/s with 136 muscles and doubled lower-body strength. Schumacher et al. reached 5.44 m/s on MyoLeg, best of 20 rollouts. None reports five-seed medians at fixed strength.

The simulator is a first-order risk. In Bolt's ablation, MuJoCo's constraint solver for contacts and joint limits prevented realistic sprinting, and MyoLeg runs with strong lateral torso oscillation (Schumacher et al.). Validate contacts and limits before blaming the controller.

Lambda-Hold's gain splits into two parts. Holding alone (excitation-hold) returns about 10x plain SAC; the lambda-space reflex adds more than another 10x (returns are exponential in speed). The direct-excitation human should therefore use the same GRF holds, which matches their excitation-hold ablation.

Exploration results depend on regime. gSDE and DEP worked at CPU scale (Lambda-Hold, Schumacher et al.) but gave no gain under large-batch GPU FastTD3 (Bolt). Report exploration together with batch size and throughput, not as a universal winner.

Muscle physiology sets the speed ceiling: force-velocity (Miller 2012; Lambda-Hold's hip flexors fall to 26-33% of isometric force) and hip strength (Yang 2026). Freezing strength, maximum shortening velocity and activation time constants is what makes the 4.0 m/s gate meaningful.

No sprint RL paper found models fatigue. MyoSuite (v2.4.0 and later) and KINESIS ship 3CC-r, but its default parameters come from elbow isometric data. Calibrate it before making any claim about the second 100 m of a 200 m.

Holding on gait events is one design choice among several: learned durations (TempoRL), per-dimension act-or-repeat (SDAR, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2502.06919) and state-deviation-triggered repeats (Safe Action Repetition, NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2111.03941). None has been tested on musculoskeletal gait.

The equilibrium-point hypothesis is actively contested (Mangalam & Stergiou 2026, Exp Brain Res, doi 10.1007/s00221-026-07242-9, plus a published comment and reply). Present lambda control as a control representation, not as evidence about the nervous system.
occupied_claims: Human-like sprinting from a minimal forward-velocity reward, with lambda thresholds and GRF-event holds in a 90-muscle 3D model (Lambda-Hold, arXiv 2608.17030). Do not headline 'first minimal-reward muscle sprint'.
Demonstration-free direct-excitation sprinting at elite speed via GPU simulation and FastTD3, with doubled strength (Wang et al., arXiv 2609.11083).
Maximum-speed running with DEP-RL on MyoLeg (5.44 m/s) and H2190 (6.49 m/s, strengthened) (Schumacher et al., arXiv 2309.02976 appendix).
Policy-set per-muscle target-length (PD) action space with full-body 3CC-r fatigue (MuscleVAE, SIGGRAPH Asia 2023, arXiv 2312.07340).
RL residual modulation of reflex gains for muscle-driven walking (arXiv 2609.11733). Synergy action spaces: H2190 (arXiv 2603.10474) and MyoLeg (SAR, arXiv 2307.03716).

Hip exoskeleton co-adapted with a musculoskeletal human policy across walking, turning, running and backward walking (UniExo, arXiv 2609.19690, 17 Sep 2026). The human is imitation-trained; hardware tested at treadmill speeds.
open_gaps: No lambda-control or event-held controller has been shown in MuJoCo/MyoLeg. A port with the published reward and five-seed medians would be new evidence in its own right.
Reflex transmission delays are absent from Lambda-Hold's recruitment law. Their effect on sprint speed and stability, alone or with device torque, is untested.
Nobody has compared learned or per-muscle hold timing (TempoRL/SDAR-style) with GRF-triggered holds for musculoskeletal running, on both simulation-step and decision-step axes.
Sprint-calibrated fatigue (3CC-r fitted to about 25 s maximal efforts) inside RL sprinting is untested. The second 100 m is the endpoint where assistance could matter.
Whether lambda-space holds help or hurt a co-adapting exosuit is unknown: within a hold, reflexes react to device torque without a policy update.
The sensitivity of MyoLeg sprint speed to MuJoCo contact and joint-limit settings, versus force-based contacts (Bolt's ablation), is unmeasured.
unverifiable: Excluded, WITHDRAWN: Kobayashi, bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.05.01.722167 (ablation of an equilibrium-point controller in a 34-muscle arm). Withdrawn 2026-05-18 for a flaw in its lambda recipe (no gravity compensation); the author asks that it not be cited.
Caveat, not a failed seed: Schumacher et al.'s maximum-running speeds come from the arXiv v2 appendix (Table III). Whether the iScience 2025 version keeps that appendix was not checked.
